_meta.title: Act 1 chart series — American taxation, 1913-2026
_meta.note: Series-level sources are declared once in each series' `source` block; per-point sourcing is not repeated. Where two credible sources disagree on a point, the disagreement is recorded in `conflicts` and MUST be resolved or footnoted before the chart ships.
_meta.companion_file: series-arrays.json — the chartable ARRAYS (26 series, ~1,400 data points). THIS file holds verified values plus the annotations and caveats that must ship alongside them. Phase 1 draws lines from series-arrays.json and reads the meaning here.
_meta.series_harvest: A second Phase 0 pass on 2026-08-17 harvested full time series, after the first pass established that it had verified VALUES but not assembled chartable ARRAYS. Three claims previously marked unsourced are now resolved; one Phase 0 'correction' is reversed.

top_statutory_rate.label: Top marginal individual income tax rate
top_statutory_rate.source: Tax Policy Center, Historical Highest Marginal Income Tax Rates
top_statutory_rate.source_caveat: TPC's own disclaimer, which must ship with the chart: "contains a number of simplifications and ignores factors such as income thresholds or deduction values"
top_statutory_rate.series_extension_note: 2024-2026 are NOT from the TPC PDF (which ends at 2023). 2024-2025 from Tax Foundation historical brackets (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/federal/historical-income-tax-rates-brackets/, updated 2026-03-18); 2026 from IRS IR-2025-103. Flag the join in the chart's source note.

annotations.1944_peak: 94% on income over $200,000 — the all-time peak. The postwar peak is 94%, NOT 91%; 1951 was also 91% and 1952-53 were 92%.
annotations.1954_1963: 91% — but see effective_rate_top_earners below. This is where the tool's core honesty note lives.
annotations.1968_1970: The '1965-81 = 70%' framing is wrong for four years: 1968 = 75.25%, 1969 = 77%, 1970 = 71.75% (Vietnam surcharge), 1981 = 69.13% (ERTA phase-in).
annotations.1988_1990: Nominal top rate 28%, but the schedule contained a 33% 'bubble' rate that phased out lower brackets — the true top marginal rate for a band of taxpayers was 33%, not 28%. Do not annotate this era as a clean 28%.

conflicts.resolution: UNRESOLVED — pick one source end-to-end or footnote
UNRESOLVED — the largest of the four conflicts
Both defensible: TPC applies JGTRRA's rate retroactively to full-year 2003; Tax Foundation shows the enacted schedule. Footnote it.

top_bracket_thresholds_mfj.label: Income threshold at which the top rate begins, married filing jointly, nominal dollars
top_bracket_thresholds_mfj.source: Tax Foundation, Federal Individual Income Tax Rates History (nominal dollars)
top_bracket_thresholds_mfj.note: Use Tax Foundation for THRESHOLDS and TPC for the RATE LINE, or commit to one source for both. The threshold series is what makes the 94% rate legible — 94% applied above $200,000 in 1944, roughly $3.6M in today's terms, which is why almost nobody paid it. CORRECTED 2026-08-18 (review fix pass): rates re-aligned to the verified TPC rate line (1934-35 = 63%; 39.6% runs 1993-2000; 39.1% = 2001; 38.6% = 2002). The 2003 entry (35%, threshold $311,950 per Tax Foundation nominal tables) was NOT added because the threshold was not re-extracted from the source PDF this pass — extract before charting this series.

current_law_2026.label: Current law after OBBBA (P.L. 119-21)
current_law_2026.source: IRS, Tax inflation adjustments for tax year 2026 including amendments from the One Big Beautiful Bill (IR-2025-103); Rev. Proc. 2025-32
current_law_2026.quote: For tax year 2026, the top tax rate remains 37% for individual single taxpayers with incomes greater than $640,600 ($768,700 for married couples filing jointly).

capital_gains_2026.note: NIIT thresholds ($200,000 single / $250,000 MFJ) are NOT inflation-indexed and were not re-verified from a 2026 primary source.

estate_exemption_2026.quote: Estates of decedents who die during 2026 have a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000, up from a total of $13,990,000 for estates of decedents who died in 2025.

current_law_2026.note: OBBBA's permanence is confirmed operationally via IRS guidance, not from the statutory text of P.L. 119-21, which was not retrieved. See blocked.json.

effective_rate_top_earners.label: What the rich actually paid — the loophole story
effective_rate_top_earners.note: THIS IS THE TOOL'S CENTRAL HONESTY EXHIBIT. Chart the statutory line and this line together; the gap between them is Act 1's bridge into Act 2.

piketty_saez_top_001pct_total_federal_19.source: Piketty & Saez, How Progressive is the U.S. Federal Tax System? A Historical and International Perspective, JEP 21(1)
piketty_saez_top_001pct_total_federal_19.quote: the top 0.01 percent of earners paid over 70 percent of their income in federal taxes in 1960
piketty_saez_top_001pct_total_federal_19.note: DEFINITION IS LOAD-BEARING and must ship inline: this is the TOTAL federal rate across four taxes — individual income + payroll + corporate income + estate and gift — with corporate and estate taxes IMPUTED to individuals as owners. These are not taxes the filer writes a check for. Income base excludes government transfers. The dossier's '~71%' should be written as 'over 70 percent', the authors' own phrasing.

piketty_saez_top_001pct_total_federal_20.quote: they paid only about 35 percent of their income in 2005
piketty_saez_top_001pct_total_federal_20.note: Computed by applying 2004 law to 2000 incomes.

piketty_saez_individual_income_component.quote: The average individual income tax rate in 1960 reached an average rate of 31 percent at the very top
piketty_saez_individual_income_component.note: THE honesty number. Statutory top rate in 1960: 91%. Actual average individual income tax rate at the very top: 31%. And most of the subsequent fall in the TOTAL rate (>70% to ~35%) came from the collapse of the imputed corporate and estate components — the individual income component fell only ~31% to ~26%. A tool that says 'the rich used to pay 91%' is wrong; a tool that says 'the rich used to pay a much higher TOTAL federal rate, mostly through corporate and estate taxes that have since shrunk' is right and more interesting.

tax_foundation_top1pct_1950s.source: Tax Foundation, Taxes on the Rich Were Not That Much Higher in the 1950s (Scott Greenberg)
tax_foundation_top1pct_1950s.quote: paid an average effective rate of only 16.9 percent in income taxes during the 1950s
tax_foundation_top1pct_1950s.all_in_comparison: Same article: the 1950s top 1% paid 'an average of 42.0 percent of their income in federal, state, and local taxes' vs '36.4 percent' in 2014.
tax_foundation_top1pct_1950s.top_01pct: Companion piece (Erica York, 2019-01-31): 'In the 1950s, the top 0.1 percent of households faced average effective income tax rates of 21.0 percent, versus 20.7 percent as of 2014.'

filers_in_the_91pct_bracket.source: Tax Foundation citing a Wall Street Journal article
filers_in_the_91pct_bracket.quote: Only a small number of taxpayers would have had enough income to fall into the top bracket – fewer than 10,000 households, according to an article in The Wall Street Journal.
filers_in_the_91pct_bracket.note: DO NOT SHIP 'a few hundred'. The verified figure is an order of magnitude larger, and it is a secondary citation of a WSJ count that was not itself retrieved. Phrase as 'fewer than 10,000 households' and attribute to Tax Foundation citing the WSJ.

effective_rate_top_earners.why_the_gap: Capital gains capped at 25%, income shifting into corporations, oil depletion allowances, real-estate shelters. The 91% rate applied only above $200,000 (~$2 million in 2017 dollars per Tax Foundation).
effective_rate_top_earners.full_matrix: RESOLVED. Piketty-Saez effective total federal rate by income group for 1960/1970/1980/1990/2000/2004 across 11 groups, plus component breakdowns for 1970 and 2004, now in series-arrays.json > piketty_saez_effective_rates.

corporate_rate.label: Top corporate income tax rate
corporate_rate.dossier_error: The dossier put 34% at 1987. TRA86's new structure took effect for tax year 1988; 1987 was a blended transition year.
corporate_rate.source: Tax Foundation, Historical Corporate Income Tax Rates & Brackets

series.note: TRANSITION YEAR — blended. Label it as such on the chart, do not plot 34%.
flat, per TCJA P.L. 115-97; no OBBBA change to the corporate rate found

corporate_rate.quote_1987: The Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86) established a new rate structure effective for Tax Year 1988 and made the rates for Transition Year 1987 an average of the pre-TRA rates for 1986 and the post-TRA rates for 1988.
corporate_rate.quote_2018: the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L. 115-97) replaced the graduated corporate tax structure with a flat 21% corporate tax rate
corporate_rate.full_series: RESOLVED. Full bracket schedules 1909-2026 in series-arrays.json > corporate_top_rate. 1940 still needs re-verification.

corporate_share_of_revenue.label: Corporate income tax as a share of total federal revenue

points.source: Tax Policy Center Briefing Book, What are the sources of revenue for the federal government?
points.quote: about one-third of the total in the early 1950s
9 percent of federal government revenue in 2022

points.note: DERIVED, not quoted: CBO's $452B corporate receipts / $5,235B total. Label as a derivation or use the 2022 TPC figure instead.

corporate_share_of_revenue.offsetting_shift: Same TPC page: individual income tax was '54 percent of total revenues' (2022); payroll taxes '30 percent of federal revenue in 2022,' historically 'nearly one-third of revenue since the early 1990s, compared with under 15 percent in the 1950s.' The corporate share did not vanish into thin air — payroll took its place. That substitution IS the regressivity story.
corporate_share_of_revenue.full_series: RESOLVED, AND UPGRADED. The complete OMB Table 2.2 receipts-by-source composition, FY1934-2023 actuals, is now in series-arrays.json > receipts_by_source. This replaces the four scattered points and is a far stronger exhibit: corporate fell 32.1% (FY1952) to 9.4% (FY2023) while payroll rose 9.7% to 36.4%. The derived FY2025 figures previously stored here should be dropped in favour of the sourced series.

payroll.label: Federal payroll tax rate and wage cap
payroll.source: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary

milestones.note: 6.2% OASDI + 1.45% HI on each side (7.65% each); self-employed pay 12.4% + 2.9% = 15.3%

milestones.quote: Beginning in 2013, an additional HI tax of 0.9 percent is assessed on earned income exceeding $125,000 for each married individual filing separately, $200,000 for individuals filing as single, and $250,000 for married couples filing jointly.
milestones.note: CORRECTION: $200,000 is the SINGLE filer threshold, not a universal one. MFJ is $250,000. Say 'above $200,000 for single filers'.

payroll.note: The SSA rate page was last updated 2013, but the schedule has not changed since 1990. Payroll is the largest federal tax for most households — a fact the top-rate chart alone conceals.
payroll.full_series: RESOLVED. Complete cap series 1937-2026 (90 points) and the full combined-rate schedule are now in series-arrays.json > payroll_cap and > payroll_rate_combined.

capital_gains_rate.label: Top long-term capital gains rate
capital_gains_rate.source: Tax Foundation, Federal Capital Gains Tax Collections, Historical Data
capital_gains_rate.methodology_quote: The maximum tax rate includes effects of exclusions (1954-1986), alternative tax rates (1954-1986; 1991-1996), the minimum tax (1970-1978)
capital_gains_rate.important: This is an EFFECTIVE-rate-inclusive series and it does NOT match the headline statutory rates. TF shows 1997 = 21.19% (not 20%), 2003 = 16.05% (not 15%), 2013 = 25.10% (not 23.8%) because it folds in the Pease limitation and personal exemption phase-outs. If the tool wants the clean statutory series (20/28/20/15/23.8), it must say so explicitly and cite a statutory source — not this table. Mixing them silently is a correctness bug.
capital_gains_rate.split_rate_years: 1978, 1981, 1997, 2003 show two values because the rate changed mid-year.
capital_gains_rate.full_series: RESOLVED. Two complete series now in series-arrays.json: capital_gains_effective (1913-2025, 113 points) and capital_gains_statutory (1913-2026). The tool must pick one and say which — see the why_two_series note there.

estate_tax.label: Federal estate tax

top_rate_1941_1976.source: IRS Statistics of Income, The Estate Tax: Ninety Years and Counting (Jacobson, Raub & Johnson)
top_rate_1941_1976.note: STRONG CHART ANNOTATION: the $60,000 exemption held flat for 34 years with no inflation indexing. Inflation did the repealing that Congress did not.

estate_tax.exemption_series_note: Use $13,990,000 for 2025. The dossier's '~$13.6M in 2024' was not verified this session — drop the 2024 point or source it separately.

share_of_deaths_taxed.source: Tax Policy Center Briefing Book, How many people pay the estate tax?
share_of_deaths_taxed.quote: only about 4,000 will be taxable—less than 0.2 percent of the 2.8 million people expected to die
share_of_deaths_taxed.note: TPC says 'less than 0.2 percent'. Do not tighten it to 0.1%. The ~4,000 estates figure IS verified.

comparison_2001.quote: Fewer than half—about 50,500—of those estates had any estate tax liability
comparison_2001.note: The ~2% share-of-deaths denominator (total 2001 deaths) was NOT retrieved. State the numerator (~50,500 taxable estates in 2001 vs ~4,000 today) rather than the percentage, or source the denominator first.

estate_tax.full_series: RESOLVED. Exemption + top rate 1916-2026 (111 points) and returns filed/taxable 2001-2022 now in series-arrays.json > estate_tax and > estate_returns.

receipts_pct_gdp.label: Federal receipts as a share of GDP ("Hauser's law")

fifty_year_average.source: CBO, The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036
fifty_year_average.quote: Revenues in 2026 total 17.5 percent of GDP, surpassing their 50-year average of 17.3 percent.
fifty_year_average.note: IMPORTANT: 17.3% is CBO's FIFTY-YEAR average (roughly 1976-2025), NOT a post-1945 average. Do not label it 'since 1945.'

recent.quote: Revenues in 2025 total 17.2 percent of GDP

range_14_5_to_20.source: OMB via FRED series FYFRGDA188S, full 1929-2025 annual series
range_14_5_to_20.note: The dossier's 14.5-20% was WRONG AT BOTH ENDS. The honest statement is: since 1945 federal receipts have stayed within roughly 13.2% and 19.8% of GDP. If you exclude 1945 itself as a demobilization year, the max is 19.8% in 2000. Runner-up context so the claim can be stated robustly: max — 1945 19.81, 2000 19.76, 1944 19.49, 2001 18.82, 2022 18.80; min — 1950 13.16, 2010 14.37, 1949 14.47, 2009 14.54.
range_14_5_to_20.fiscal_magnitude: At CBO's projected 2026 GDP of $31,902B, one percentage point is about $319B/yr, so the 6.6-point post-1945 range is worth roughly $2.1 trillion a year. The flat line does NOT mean rates do not matter.

income_distribution.label: Top 1% share of pre-tax income — two credible series that disagree
income_distribution.note: SHIP BOTH, LABELED. Direction is shared; magnitude is genuinely contested. Never average them. This is causal-honesty note #6.

piketty_saez.source: Emmanuel Saez, Striking it Richer: The Evolution of Top Incomes in the United States

points.quote: a peak to almost 24 percent in the late 1920s
By 2022, the top 1% income share stays very elevated 23.6%

piketty_saez.critical_note: ALL FOUR FIGURES INCLUDE REALIZED CAPITAL GAINS. The current value is 23.6%, NOT the dossier's '20-21%' — that figure is the series EXCLUDING capital gains, which was not retrieved. The chart must label which variant it plots; mixing them produces a false 3-point jump. Latest year available is 2022.

auten_splinter.source: Auten & Splinter, Income Inequality in the United States: Extensions and Updates; flagship article JPE 132(7) 2024
auten_splinter.headline_finding_quote: after-tax top income shares declined in the late 1960s and increased in the late 1980s and 1990s. However, after-tax top income shares are little changed relative to the early 1960s.
auten_splinter.jpe_quote: top income shares are lower and have increased less since 1980 than other studies using tax data
auten_splinter.note: The dossier's 13-14% / 8.8% are an older vintage. The May 2025 update puts 2022 at 15.5% / 10.3%. The 'little rise in the after-tax share since the early 1960s' finding IS verified verbatim.

income_distribution.the_honest_framing: Two credible tax-data series differ by roughly 8 points on the SAME year: Saez 23.6% vs Auten-Splinter 15.5% pre-tax, 2022. Roughly two-thirds of the gap is who gets assigned untaxed business income; the rest is treatment of missing income, tax-base changes, and declining marriage rates. CBO's own series is the safe middle path to embed as primary, with these two as labeled alternates.

psz_after_tax_comparator.note: The direct PSZ after-tax comparator (~15%) appears only in Figure 4B of the Auten-Splinter update, without quoted values. Do not publish the PSZ vs AS after-tax pair until sourced.

income_distribution.full_series: RESOLVED. THREE competing series now stored in full: series-arrays.json > top_income_share_wid (1913-2024, 112 pts), > top_income_share_piketty_saez_fiscal (1913-1998, 86 pts, both capital-gains variants), > top_income_share_auten_splinter (1960-2022, 60 pts). Three different definitions — never splice or average them.

cbo_distribution_2022.label: CBO, The Distribution of Household Income, 2022
cbo_distribution_2022.critical_note: RESOLVED 2026-08-17 — the supplemental spreadsheet was obtained and parsed. See data/cbo-distribution.json for the full 1979-2022 series.

average_federal_tax_rate_all.quote: In 2022, the average federal tax rate for all households in the United States was 20.6 percent

top_quintile_share_of_federal_taxes.quote: The share of federal taxes paid by households in the top quintile increased from 55 percent in 1979 to 70 percent in 2022

top_1pct_share_of_federal_taxes.quote: The share of federal taxes paid by households in the top 1 percent of the income distribution, which grew by 13 percentage points—from 14 percent in 1979 to 27 percent in 2022
top_1pct_share_of_federal_taxes.unrounded_source: Tax Foundation reading of the CBO data

top_1pct_share_of_pretax_income.quote: the share of income before transfers and taxes going to households in the top 1 percent of the distribution increased from 9 percent to 18 percent

individual_income_tax_rate_range.quote: average individual income tax rates ranged from −10 percent in the lowest quintile to 17 percent in the highest quintile
individual_income_tax_rate_range.note: INCOME TAX ONLY — distinct from the total federal rates below, which include payroll, corporate, and excise. The negative rate in the lowest quintile is refundable credits (EITC/CTC).

total_federal_tax_rate_by_group.source: CBO 61911 supplemental data, Table 9 (primary) — supersedes the Tax Foundation secondary reading
total_federal_tax_rate_by_group.quote: The effective federal tax rate rose from 1.4 percent for the bottom quintile to 23.2 percent for the top quintile and 31.5 percent for the top 1 percent
total_federal_tax_rate_by_group.non_monotonic_note: Worth preserving: the top 1% rate (31.5%) is NOT the highest sub-group. The 99.9th-99.99th percentile pays 32.6% while the top 0.01% pays 31.2%. The very top pays a LOWER rate than the merely very rich — which is the realization-doctrine story in one data point.
total_federal_tax_rate_by_group.CORRECTION: SECONDARY SOURCE WAS WRONG ON ONE CELL. Tax Foundation, reading CBO 61911, published '1.4 percent for the bottom quintile to 23.2 percent for the top quintile and 31.5 percent for the top 1 percent'. CBO's own supplemental data gives the HIGHEST QUINTILE as 25.9 percent, not 23.2. The bottom quintile (1.4) and top 1 percent (31.5) match exactly, as do the tax shares (70.2 and 27.3). Use 25.9 and cite CBO directly. Two of three right and one wrong is exactly why the primary was worth getting.

by_component_2022.note: CBO Table 9 also breaks every group into individual income / payroll / corporate / excise. Full series in cbo-distribution.json.

payroll_tax_rate_by_quintile.note: Payroll taxes are REGRESSIVE across this span: 9.5% at the bottom, 6.1% at the top.

share_data.quote: the bottom 60 percent of taxpayers paid only 3.3 percent of federal taxes in 2020 and 1.3 percent in 2021, but that rose to 12.8 percent of federal taxes in 2022.
share_data.warning: STRONG CAUTION AGAINST USING 2020 OR 2021 AS A BASELINE YEAR. The bottom-60% federal tax share was 3.3% (2020) and 1.3% (2021) purely because of pandemic recovery rebate credits, rebounding to 12.8% in 2022. Any comparison anchored on 2020-21 is measuring the pandemic, not the tax code.

historical_series.citation_error: THAT CITATION IS WRONG AND MUST BE REMOVED. CBO publication 61259 is 'H.R. 1491, Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act' (2025-03-24), a bill cost estimate with no distributional data whatsoever.

partial_evidence.bottom_quintile: The effective federal tax rate for the bottom quintile averaged about 10.6 percent in the 1980s but has remained below 3 percent since 2007.

historical_series.note: The dossier's endpoints ('top 1% ~33% in 1979 to ~30% in 2021; middle quintile ~19% to ~13%; lowest ~10% to 0-3%') are UNVERIFIED. The honest phrasing available today for the bottom quintile is 'about 10.6 percent averaged across the 1980s, falling to 1.4 percent in 2022' — anchored on a decade average, not a 1979 point. Note also that 2021 is a distorted pandemic year and 2022 is the better endpoint; the verified 2022 top-1% rate of 31.5% makes the dossier's 'declining to ~30%' narrative misleading.
historical_series.breakthrough: CBO's OLDER reports publish the quintile series as extractable PDF tables. Now in series-arrays.json > cbo_effective_rates_historical: total effective rate by group 1979-2005 (27 years x 9 groups), and rates BY COMPONENT plus SHARES of total federal tax liabilities 1979-2002 (24 years x 9 groups x 10 measures). The dossier's claim that this needed a spreadsheet was true only for post-2002 vintages. Still blocked: 2003-2021.

soi_percentiles.label: IRS Statistics of Income — who pays federal income tax, TY2023
soi_percentiles.source: Tax Foundation, Who Pays Federal Income Taxes (reading IRS SOI Table 4.1)
soi_percentiles.cross_check: Independently reproduced by National Taxpayers Union Foundation (https://www.ntu.org/foundation/detail/who-pays-income-taxes-tax-year-2023, 2026-04-14) with identical values.
soi_percentiles.universe: All individual returns EXCLUDING dependent returns — 153,076,443 returns. NOT the same universe as SOI's all-returns tables (160.7M in TY2022).
soi_percentiles.quote: The top 1 percent earned 20.6 percent of total AGI and paid 38.4 percent of all federal income taxes.
soi_percentiles.quote_2: The top 1 percent of taxpayers paid a 26.3 percent average rate, seven times higher than the 3.7 percent average rate paid by the bottom half
soi_percentiles.ntu_quote: more than 49 million tax returns in 2023 reported no income tax liability—30.5% of all returns.
soi_percentiles.critical_note: THIS IS INCOME TAX ONLY. It excludes payroll tax, which is the largest federal tax for most of the bottom half. Presenting the '3.73% average rate for the bottom 50%' without the payroll figure alongside it would be the single most misleading thing this tool could do. Pair it with CBO's total-federal-rate series (cbo_distribution_2022) every time.
soi_percentiles.sub_1pct_blocked: Top 0.1% and top 0.01% breakouts are BLOCKED — they exist only in SOI Table 4.1 (.xlsx). Neither Tax Foundation nor NTU publishes below the top 1%.

soi_agi_classes_ty2022.label: IRS SOI, income and tax by AGI size class — TY2022 PRELIMINARY (fallback only)
soi_agi_classes_ty2022.source: IRS SOI Bulletin, Individual Income Tax Returns, Preliminary Data, Tax Year 2022
soi_agi_classes_ty2022.units: thousands of dollars; returns are counts
soi_agi_classes_ty2022.universe: ALL returns (160,728,129) — a DIFFERENT universe from soi_percentiles above, which excludes dependents (153,076,443). Do not mix them.
soi_agi_classes_ty2022.note: INADEQUATE AS THE ENGINE'S LAYER-1 BASE. The top bracket is a single '$250,000 or more' bucket — no $500k / $1M / $5M / $10M splits — so it cannot support a top-rate slider with a bracket threshold, which is Act 2's headline lever. The real base is SOI Table 3.5 (TY2023), which is blocked. See blocked.json item 2.

absolute_mobility.label: Share of children out-earning their parents
absolute_mobility.status: PHASE 0 CORRECTION REVERSED — the dossier was right
absolute_mobility.phase0_first_pass_said: CORRECTED: use 'approximately 90%' and 'the 1980s'; the 92%/1984 pairing is a secondary-retelling error not in the paper
absolute_mobility.second_pass_finding: BOTH FIGURES ARE VERBATIM IN THE SAME PAPER. The abstract rounds and generalizes; the body is precise.
absolute_mobility.abstract_quote: We found that rates of absolute mobility have fallen from approximately 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in the 1980s.
absolute_mobility.body_quote: the fraction of children earning more than their parents fell from 92% in the 1940 birth cohort to 50% in the 1984 birth cohort
absolute_mobility.resolution: USE 92% AND THE 1984 COHORT, citing the paper's body — it is the more precise statement and it is what the dossier said. Alternatively use ~90% / 'the 1980s' citing the abstract. DO NOT MIX the two framings.
absolute_mobility.source: Chetty, Grusky, Hell, Hendren, Manduca & Narang, The fading American dream, Science 356(6336):398
absolute_mobility.full_series_status: BLOCKED — the cohort-by-cohort array lives only in Opportunity Insights .dta/.xlsx files. Only the two endpoints are chartable.

life_expectancy_gap.label: Life expectancy gap between richest and poorest 1%
life_expectancy_gap.source: Chetty et al., The Association Between Income and Life Expectancy in the United States, 2001-2014, JAMA 315(16):1750-66
life_expectancy_gap.quote: The gap in life expectancy between the richest 1% and poorest 1% of individuals was 14.6 years (95% CI, 14.4 to 14.8 years) for men and 10.1 years (95% CI, 9.9 to 10.3 years) for women.
life_expectancy_gap.note: Cite the study window (2001-2014); this is not a current-year figure.

top_1pct_wealth_share.source: Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts via FRED series WFRBST01134
top_1pct_wealth_share.note: Share of NET WORTH, not income. Quarterly and revises — date-stamp the chart.

real_median_household_income.source: Census Bureau, Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2024 (CB25-TPS.62); report P60-286
real_median_household_income.quote: Real median household income was $83,730 in 2024, not statistically different from the 2023 estimate of $82,690.
real_median_household_income.note: THE 'RECORD' CLAIM MUST BE QUALIFIED. Census explicitly says it is not statistically different from 2023. Say 'highest on record but not statistically different from 2023,' or drop the word record. 2025 data is not yet published (expected ~September 2026); build the tool to accept the update.

home_price_to_income.source: Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies (Hermann & Whitney), Home Price-to-Income Ratio Reaches Record High
home_price_to_income.quote: In 2022, the median sale price for a single-family home in the US was 5.6 times higher than the median household income

comparator_2019.quote: As recently as 2019, the national price-to-income ratio was just 4.1

home_price_to_income.note: The 2022 record of 5.6 IS verified. The dossier's '2.2-3.0 from 1950-1985' is NOT — JCHS says its data go back only to the early 1970s. The nearest supporting datum: in 2000 'fully two-thirds of large markets had price-to-income ratios below 3.0.' Either drop the pre-1970 range or label it unsourced. A newer State of the Nation's Housing 2026 exists but its numeric ratio was not retrievable.

public_college_tuition.status: RESOLVED — was unsourced; the dossier's framing was also WRONG IN DIRECTION
public_college_tuition.dossier_claimed: real public college tuition roughly tripled 1980-2020

verified.series: NCES Digest Table 330.10, published tuition and fees, public 4-year, constant 2023-24 dollars, 1963-64 through 2023-24

public_college_tuition.correction: Real published tuition roughly QUADRUPLED from 1980-81 to its 2015-16 peak — not tripled — and then FELL about 13% through 2023-24. A series ending in 2020 is cherry-picked near the peak.
public_college_tuition.mandatory_pairing: PUBLISHED PRICE IS NOT NET PRICE, and they tell opposite recent stories. College Board: average NET tuition and fees for first-time full-time in-state students at public four-years peaked in 2012-13 at $4,450 (2025 dollars) and fell to an estimated $2,300 in 2025-26 — a ~48% real decline. THE TOOL MUST SHOW BOTH OR NEITHER. Showing published price alone would be the weakest, most attackable claim on the page.

productivity_pay_gap.source: Economic Policy Institute, The Productivity-Pay Gap
productivity_pay_gap.note: EPI's tracker moves with each quarterly release — date-stamp any figure taken from it. EPI's own site elsewhere says 'Productivity has grown 3.5 times as much as pay,' which does NOT match the 2.8x implied by the current tracker numbers; cite the tracker figures and the 2.8x ratio.

mandatory_caveat.source: Stansbury & Summers, Productivity and Pay: Is the link broken?, NBER Working Paper 24165
mandatory_caveat.quote: Since 1973 median compensation has diverged starkly from average labor productivity. Since 2000, average compensation has also begun to diverge from labor productivity.
mandatory_caveat.finding: They find a one-percentage-point rise in productivity growth is associated with 0.7-1.0 points higher median/average compensation growth — i.e. the productivity-pay LINK is largely intact, and the divergence reflects forces acting on pay independent of productivity, not a broken link.
mandatory_caveat.note: The deflator-choice, benefits-inclusion, and median-vs-average critiques are real and commonly attributed to this literature, but were NOT found verbatim in the retrieved abstract. Attribute them cautiously or fetch the full PDF first. This is causal-honesty note #7.

causal_honesty_notes._note: These ship as VISIBLE UI COPY attached to the relevant chart moments — a hard requirement per gameplan §4, not polish. Numbers referenced here are sourced elsewhere in this file.
causal_honesty_notes.1_91pct_and_the_1950s_boom: Effective rates were far lower than statutory (top 1% paid 16.9% in income tax; the top 0.01% paid over 70% only counting imputed corporate and estate taxes), and growth had other drivers — the postwar international position, demographics, cheap energy. Say 'high rates did not prevent fast growth,' never 'caused it.'
causal_honesty_notes.2_reagan_cuts_and_the_1980s_recovery: The rebound tracked Volcker disinflation and large deficits; top-rate-specific growth evidence is weak; taxes were raised repeatedly after 1981.
causal_honesty_notes.3_clinton_1993_and_the_1990s_boom: The mirror fallacy. The honest claim is only that the 1993 increase demonstrably did not abort growth.
causal_honesty_notes.4_tax_cuts_pay_for_themselves: No major US cut has. See parameters.json > growth_feedback: verified offsets run 1-32%, and CRFB's arithmetic is the intuition pump — a policy would need to produce $5 to $6 of economic activity per $1 of cost to self-finance. Kansas and its bipartisan repeal is the cleanest exhibit.
causal_honesty_notes.5_hausers_law: Flatness in receipts/GDP does not mean rates do not matter — the composition shifted (payroll up, corporate down) and the range is fiscally enormous. NOTE: the dossier's 14.5-20% range is unsourced; use the verified 2022 (18.80%) vs 2023 (15.97%) contrast instead until the full series is retrieved.
causal_honesty_notes.6_inequality_is_contested: Piketty-Saez 23.6% vs Auten-Splinter 15.5% for the SAME year (2022). Direction shared, magnitude disputed. Show both, never average.
causal_honesty_notes.7_productivity_pay_chart: Disclose the deflator, benefits, and median-vs-average caveats; Stansbury & Summers find the productivity-pay link largely intact, with the divergence driven by forces acting on pay independent of productivity.
causal_honesty_notes.8_the_robust_association: The one association that IS robust: cutting top rates correlates with rising top-1% income share (Hungerford CRS R42729; Piketty-Saez-Stantcheva AEJ:EP 2014; Hope & Limberg 2022). State it confidently while flagging that the mechanism is debated. NOT RE-VERIFIED IN PHASE 0 — these three citations came from the dossier and were not in the verification queue. Verify before shipping the claim.
causal_honesty_notes.9_1950s_nostalgia: Requires the exclusion caveats in the same sentence, not a footnote: Black median family income ~55% of white; redlining and FHA exclusion; women excluded from credit; homes ~1,000 sq ft; healthcare ~5% of GDP because medicine could do little. NOT RE-VERIFIED IN PHASE 0 — these figures came from the dossier's §B8 and were not in the queue. Verify before shipping. ALSO: the '~33% union density' figure uses union members as a share of NONAGRICULTURAL WAGE AND SALARY employment. On the total-employed denominator in series-arrays.json > union_density the 1950s peak is 28.3% (1954). If the era card says 33%, source it separately — do not cite that array for it.

bracket_thresholds_ty2023.label: Taxable-income threshold at which the 37% top rate begins, tax year 2023
bracket_thresholds_ty2023.source: IRS, Revenue Procedure 2022-38 (inflation-adjusted items for tax year 2023), Section 3.01 Tax Rate Tables

married_filing_jointly.quote: Over $693,750 $186,601.50 plus 37% of the excess over $693,750

unmarried.quote: Over $578,125 $174,238.25 plus 37% of the excess over $578,125

bracket_thresholds_ty2023.added: 2026-08-17, Phase 2. The only figure added to data/ after Phase 0; verified against the IRS primary with a verbatim quote, per the project's own sourcing rule.
bracket_thresholds_ty2023.why_it_was_needed: The Act 2 top-rate lever offers a NEW bracket at a higher dollar threshold. Without the current bracket start, the engine can only raise the rate on ALL income already in the top bracket, which for a '70% above $10 million' setting overstates the base roughly three-fold against published scores (Tax Foundation $291.7B conventional, Penn Wharton $382.3B static). With it, the engine computes income above the user's threshold as (income taxed at 37%) minus (returns x (threshold - bracket start)) and lands within about 10% of the Tax Foundation figure.
bracket_thresholds_ty2023.engine_use: The engine uses the MARRIED-FILING-JOINTLY threshold. SOI Table 3.5 is all returns with filing statuses combined (the by-status table is 3.4), so one threshold has to be chosen; joint returns dominate the AGI classes above $1 million. Using the unmarried threshold instead would subtract about $115,000 more per return, lowering the computed base slightly.
